name: Rosyth
title: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging at Rosyth | Drydock and Basin
description: Ship thickness measurement at Rosyth for ferries, offshore vessels and cargo ships docking at the Babcock yard: shell, double bottom, tank and piping UTM.
h1: Thickness Gauging for Commercial Ships Docking at Rosyth
intro: Rosyth, on the Fife shore of the Forth just upstream of the bridges, is home to Babcock's dockyard, where aircraft carriers are maintained and frigates built, and where commercial ships also come in for drydocking. Forth Ports runs a cargo terminal next door. For owners, Rosyth matters as a docking yard: the hull is dry, staging is up and the class surveyor attends. Atlantis mobilises technicians from India to work through the dock period on the owner's behalf, keeping pace with the yard.

highlights.p: Rosyth's docks handle the largest warships the Royal Navy operates, and the yard also takes commercial vessels such as island ferries. A dry hull gives access to bottom plating, sea chests and the stern area, which is exactly what a renewal or docking survey needs gauged.

A dock period is short and every day in it counts, so gauging has to keep pace with blasting, staging and the surveyor's visits. We work to the yard's sequence and report substantial corrosion daily, so that steel renewal can start straight away.

The dockyard is also a defence site, so access for visiting technicians is controlled more tightly than at a commercial port. We send passport details and the job scope to the yard and the owner's representative early, so passes are ready when the ship enters dock.

port.h: Rosyth: a naval dockyard that also docks merchant ships
p: Rosyth lies on the northern shore of the Firth of Forth in Fife, just west of the Forth Bridge, the Forth Road Bridge and the Queensferry Crossing, and within easy reach of Edinburgh across the river. The dockyard was built as a naval base in the early twentieth century and is now owned and run by Babcock. Its approach from the Forth leads to a basin entered through a lock, from which the drydocks open, and the entrance was widened so that the Queen Elizabeth-class aircraft carriers could be assembled in the yard and floated out. Ships arrive with a Forth pilot and tugs, and moving a vessel through the lock and into dock is planned around the tide, which makes the timetable of a docking at Rosyth more fixed than at an open-water yard.

Most of the yard's work is naval. Babcock maintains the aircraft carriers in the large dock under a long-term contract, builds the Royal Navy's Type 31 frigates on the site, and manages the laid-up nuclear submarines held at Rosyth while they are dismantled. Commercial ship repair fits around that programme. The yard has docked ferries from the Scottish island services, including the NorthLink ships that run to Orkney and Shetland, and takes other merchant and offshore vessels when dock space allows. Next to the dockyard, Forth Ports operates a commercial port with berths for cargo ships, and together the two make Rosyth a place where a ship might be repaired, laid up for a spell or simply discharge her cargo.

For thickness gauging the important point is that Rosyth is mainly a docking location rather than a cargo stop. A commercial ship comes here for a planned period with a repair specification, which is the right setting for a renewal survey, a docking survey with bottom gauging, or a steel renewal programme following an earlier condition report. The Forth is sheltered at this point and weather seldom stops work inside the basin, though short winter days make the yard's temporary lighting important on deck and over the side as well as inside tanks. Owners who know a ship is due to dock here can have us take pre-docking readings at an earlier port, so the steel quantities are written into the specification before the ship arrives in the Forth.

facilities.h: Docks, basin and quays where Rosyth work takes place
p: Gauging during a Rosyth docking follows the same order as the yard. Once the dock is pumped out and the hull washed, bottom and side shell readings are taken from the dock floor and staging, sea chests are opened and measured, and the rudder and stern frame area are examined. Inside the ship, double-bottom and ballast tanks are opened, ventilated and certified safe for entry in an agreed sequence, and the team works through them with the surveyor's close-up survey programme in mind. Where plating is found below the allowable diminution, the area is marked on the steel and recorded on the class sketch the same day.

Ships waiting to enter dock, or lying afloat after undocking to finish repairs, use quays in the basin, which is a good place to complete deck, hold and piping gauging that does not need the hull to be dry. The Forth Ports berths beside the dockyard handle cargo ships, and a ship discharging there can be gauged in the normal way. Ships that call at Leith or Grangemouth before a Rosyth docking give one more opportunity, because readings taken on those calls can turn the docking specification into a firm steel list.

Dockyard basin quays — afloat repair periods for deck, hold, tank and piping work before or after docking.
Forth Ports berths at Rosyth — routine gauging on cargo ships while they discharge.
Lay-by berths in the basin — longer condition surveys on ships waiting for dock space or laid up.

context.h: Port state control, class surveys and a defence site
p: Merchant ships calling at the Forth Ports terminal at Rosyth fall under port state control by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, applied through UK law within the Paris MoU. In the dockyard itself the controlling documents are the class rules and the repair contract. The attending surveyor decides the extent of gauging for the survey due, the yard plans staging and access, and the owner's superintendent decides how far to go beyond the class minimum, for example in tanks that are not yet due for survey but are likely to need steel before the next docking.

The dockyard's role as a defence site affects visitors more than the work itself. Visiting technicians, particularly foreign nationals, go through the yard's security process before they are given access, which takes longer than a gate pass at a commercial quay, and the yard may restrict photography to what the job needs. For a team travelling from India this is planned alongside the UK visa, and the job documents name the ship, the dock dates and the scope so the yard can process the request. Ship recycling paperwork follows UK rules rather than the EU regulation, and ships trading to EU ports keep their Inventory of Hazardous Materials current for those calls.

jobs.h: What we are asked to gauge at Rosyth
jobs.p: Rosyth jobs are docking jobs. Ferry operators bring ships in for scheduled dockings and renewal surveys, offshore and cargo owners use the yard when its docks are free, and each of these needs thickness measurement planned around the dock period. We are asked to take readings for the owner's own records alongside the class programme, to extend gauging into tanks the owner suspects, to measure piping systems that are being considered for renewal, and to confirm the extent of steel renewal once plates are cut out. When the ship has called somewhere earlier, our pre-docking readings often become the basis of the yard's quotation and the steel order.
list: Renewal-survey gauging on an island ferry in the Babcock dock: shell, double bottom, car-deck plating and ballast tanks.
Bottom plating and sea chest gauging during a docking survey, with sea chest gratings and internals examined.
Car deck and ramp structure gauging on a ro-pax vessel, where wheel loads and road salt cause wear and corrosion.

logistics: Edinburgh Airport lies a short drive south of the Forth crossings, which makes Rosyth one of the easier Scottish yards to reach. Teams travel from India on UK visitor visas, and because the dockyard runs its own security clearance, we start the access paperwork with the yard and the owner as soon as the docking dates are firm. The ship's agent or the owner's site representative arranges day-to-day access; accommodation is in Dunfermline, Inverkeithing or Edinburgh, depending on the length of the docking.
vessels: Bulk carriers calling at the cargo terminal

faqs.q: Can you work on a commercial ship in the Babcock dock at Rosyth?
faqs.a: Yes, as the owner's or manager's contractor rather than the yard's. Gauging is coordinated with the yard's programme, and staging, lighting, ventilation and gas-free certificates are arranged by the yard and the superintendent. The class surveyor sets the extent of the survey, and we can extend readings into any further areas the owner wants checked while the ship is out of the water.

faqs.q: How early should we arrange access to the Rosyth dockyard?
faqs.a: As soon as the docking dates are agreed. The yard is a defence site with its own security process, and visiting foreign nationals need clearance before they arrive, on top of their UK visas. We send passport details, the ship's name, the dock dates and the scope through the owner's representative, which normally gives the yard enough time to issue access.

faqs.q: Can gauging be done before the ship arrives at Rosyth?
faqs.a: Often, and it saves dock time. If the ship calls at Leith, Grangemouth or another port before docking, we can take readings there on the areas most likely to need steel renewal. The yard then receives a measured steel estimate instead of an allowance, plates can be ordered in advance, and the dock period is spent renewing steel rather than finding it.

faqs.q: Do you gauge car decks and ramps on ferries docking here?
faqs.a: Yes. Car decks, ramps, hoistable deck supports and stern door structure take repeated wheel loads and are often wet with salt carried in by vehicles, so wastage and grooving are common. We gauge plating and stiffeners, record pitting where it occurs, and use magnetic particle testing on welds at ramp hinges and supports when the owner wants cracks ruled out.
